Unit 3 — Deriving a Triton KDA chunk and scan design
Memory summary

This unit was algorithm research and design, not implementation. The agent found that FLA’s chunked KDA flow offers a useful structural reference, but its gate scaling differs from the task oracle. After weighing an affine parallel scan against a serial state scan, the agent settled on a custom Triton intra-chunk kernel followed by a chunk-serial scan/output kernel. The unit ended with a capability probe confirming gather, cumsum, and dot support on SM 9.0. No correctness check or benchmark was run.

Relevant prior context

The actual device probe reported an 80 GB H100 with compute capability 9.0, while the problem metadata described an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell target. This unit began by checking the evaluator’s tolerances and hardware table, then cloned FLA’s public repository into /tmp to study its algorithm; it did not call a prohibited FLA operation.

Important non-obvious context
  • The reference applies a cumulative sum to g along the 64-token chunk axis without the scale used by FLA’s chunk_local_cumsum. Matching the reference requires following the oracle’s unscaled chunk-local cumsum.
  • The checker’s nominal bf16 tolerance was read as 0.05 absolute and relative. The stress overrides observed in the checker were tighter for small inputs (atol=5e-4, rtol=5e-2) and atol=5e-2, rtol=5e-2 for large inputs.
  • The trace’s score analysis used a 756 TFLOPS bf16 peak from the H100 PCIe table. That is a hardware-table figure, not a measurement of the detected SXM device or the RTX PRO 6000 target in the problem files.
  • The runtime stack was Torch 2.7.0, Triton 3.3.0, CUDA 12.8, capability 9.0. The final probe output was:
True True True
(9, 0)
  • Official score remained None, and correctness remained “not run yet” at the end of this unit.
Recording summary

The agent first inspected the checker’s tolerance logic and hardware lookup tables. It estimated the benchmark’s nominal work and considered a chunk-parallel affine scan: rewrite each chunk’s state update as S_next = S @ T + B, then compute output as P @ S + R. This formulation exposes an associative scan, but composing full (K,K) transitions would add substantial matrix work and intermediate traffic. The agent therefore judged a direct parallel scan too costly to implement as the first version.

The agent cloned FLA for source study and traced its forward into three conceptual stages: intra-chunk preparation, a recurrent state update over chunks, and output generation. FLA’s intra kernel subdivides the 64-token chunk into 16-token blocks; it solves diagonal triangular blocks with row-wise forward substitution and obtains off-diagonal blocks with matrix products. Its state kernel scans chunks serially while splitting the value dimension across programs.

The agent derived the reference’s chunk-local quantities: form kg = k * exp(g_cumsum) and kd = k * exp(-g_cumsum), use their product for the lower-triangular K/K matrix, solve for the corrected weights, and form the query/key interactions. It noted that the inverse-like correction is awkward to express with Triton row indexing. It considered FLA-style 16×16 block inversion and a full-tile gather/update loop, then chose the latter as a simpler first experiment.

The design at the end of the unit was two Triton kernels: one program per batch/head/chunk to compute intra-chunk quantities, then a kernel that scans chunks serially while maintaining the state and writing output. Value-dimension splitting remained a tuning choice. The agent planned to use Triton’s cumulative sum in the chunk kernel and test against the reference before optimizing.

No kernel code was written in this unit, and neither correctness nor performance was measured.

Hindsight (written after the run; not known at the time)
  • Fate: no_code_change. Unit 3 derived a two-kernel design but did not edit solution code.
  • Contribution: None to the score; the intra-chunk plus recurrent scan structure became the final architecture.
  • Takeaway: The design choice held up, though later work showed the direct recurrence was more reliable than matrix-composed scans.

Recording summary

The agent first decided on intermediate layouts with chunk-major storage: w, u, qg, Aqk, and kprime in bf16, plus D in fp32. The intra-chunk kernel loads q/k/v/g/beta, computes the cumulative gate, forms decayed products, constructs the lower-triangular interaction matrix, applies row substitution, then stores the intermediates. The scan kernel keeps state S in fp32 and processes chunks in sequence, computing the correction, output, and state update.

The scratch implementation used these central operations:

g_c = tl.cumsum(b_g, axis=0)
eg = tl.exp(g_c)
e_neg = tl.exp(-g_c)
kg = b_k * eg
kd = b_k * e_neg
qg = b_q * scale * eg

A_raw = tl.dot(kg, tl.trans(kd), input_precision="tf32")

It used row substitution to update the strict lower triangle, then added the identity and beta-scaled columns before computing w and u. The scan recurrence was:

b_v = b_u - tl.dot(b_w, S, input_precision="tf32")
o_tile = tl.dot(b_qg, S, input_precision="tf32") + tl.dot(b_A, b_v, input_precision="tf32")
S = S * b_D[:, None] + tl.dot(tl.trans(b_kp), b_v, input_precision="tf32")

The agent’s working hypothesis was that the intra kernel’s register use came partly from keeping several (64, 64) inverse-related tiles live at once. The original L⁴ approximation computed L² and L⁴ before building Bm. The proposed schedule builds Bm incrementally, then multiplies in each power as it becomes available:

Bm = I + L
L2 = L @ L
Bm = Bm @ (I + L2)
L4 = L2 @ L2
Bm = Bm @ (I + L4)

This keeps at most three of those tiles live at once, by the agent’s estimate, instead of five. A first attempt put the experiment in a heredoc; Triton rejected the inline JIT definition:

ValueError: @jit functions should be defined in a Python file

The agent then changed solution.py to use the interleaved schedule. The edit preserved the same power-method terms but changed their evaluation order:

# interleaved so fewer power tiles are live at once
Bm = I + L
L2 = tl.dot(L, L).to(tl.bfloat16)
Bm = tl.dot(Bm, I + L2).to(tl.bfloat16)
L4 = tl.dot(L2, L2).to(tl.bfloat16)
Bm = tl.dot(Bm, I + L4).to(tl.bfloat16)
